<p><b>Turkey</b> (<a href="/wiki/Turkish_language" title="Turkish language">Turkish</a>: <i lang="tr">Türkiye</i> <small></small><span title="Representation in the International Phonetic Alphabet (IPA)" class="IPA" lang="tr-Latn-fonipa"><a href="/wiki/Help:IPA/Turkish" title="Help:IPA/Turkish">[ˈtyɾcije]</a></span>), officially the <b>Republic of Türkiye</b> (Turkish: <i lang="tr">Türkiye Cumhuriyeti</i> <small></small><span title="Representation in the International Phonetic Alphabet (IPA)" class="IPA" lang="tr-Latn-fonipa"><a href="/wiki/Help:IPA/Turkish" title="Help:IPA/Turkish">[ˈtyɾcije dʒumˈhuːɾijeti]</a></span>&#32;<span class="nowrap" style="font-size:85%">(<span class="unicode haudio"><span class="fn"><span style="white-space:nowrap;margin-right:.25em;"><a href="/wiki/File:Tur-T%C3%BCrkiye_Cumhuriyeti.ogg" title="About this sound"><img alt="" src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/8a/Loudspeaker.svg/11px-Loudspeaker.svg.png" decoding="async" width="11" height="11" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/8a/Loudspeaker.svg/17px-Loudspeaker.svg.png 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/8a/Loudspeaker.svg/22px-Loudspeaker.svg.png 2x" data-file-width="20" data-file-height="20" /></a></span><a href="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/3/37/Tur-T%C3%BCrkiye_Cumhuriyeti.ogg" class="internal" title="Tur-Türkiye Cumhuriyeti.ogg">listen</a></span></span>)</span>), is a <a href="/wiki/List_of_transcontinental_countries" title="List of transcontinental countries">transcontinental country</a> located mainly on the <a href="/wiki/Anatolia" title="Anatolia">Anatolian Peninsula</a> in <a href="/wiki/Western_Asia" title="Western Asia">Western Asia</a>, with a <a href="/wiki/East_Thrace" title="East Thrace">small portion</a> on the <a href="/wiki/Balkans" title="Balkans">Balkan Peninsula</a> in <a href="/wiki/Southeast_Europe" title="Southeast Europe">Southeast Europe</a>. It borders the <a href="/wiki/Black_Sea" title="Black Sea">Black Sea</a> to the north; <a href="/wiki/Georgia_(country)" title="Georgia (country)">Georgia</a> to the northeast; <a href="/wiki/Armenia" title="Armenia">Armenia</a>, <a href="/wiki/Azerbaijan" title="Azerbaijan">Azerbaijan</a>, and <a href="/wiki/Iran" title="Iran">Iran</a> to the east; <a href="/wiki/Iraq" title="Iraq">Iraq</a> to the southeast; <a href="/wiki/Syria" title="Syria">Syria</a> and the <a href="/wiki/Mediterranean_Sea" title="Mediterranean Sea">Mediterranean Sea</a> to the south; the <a href="/wiki/Aegean_Sea" title="Aegean Sea">Aegean Sea</a> to the west; and <a href="/wiki/Greece" title="Greece">Greece</a> and <a href="/wiki/Bulgaria" title="Bulgaria">Bulgaria</a> to the northwest. <a href="/wiki/Cyprus" title="Cyprus">Cyprus</a> is off the south coast. Most people are <a href="/wiki/Turkish_people" title="Turkish people">Turks</a>, and <a href="/wiki/Kurds" title="Kurds">Kurds</a> are the largest minority.<sup id="cite_ref-cia_4-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-cia-4">&#91;4&#93;</a></sup> <a href="/wiki/Ankara" title="Ankara">Ankara</a> is Turkey's capital, while <a href="/wiki/Istanbul" title="Istanbul">Istanbul</a> is its <a href="/wiki/List_of_largest_cities_and_towns_in_Turkey" title="List of largest cities and towns in Turkey">largest city</a> and <a href="/wiki/Financial_centre" title="Financial centre">financial centre</a>.
</p><p>One of the world's earliest permanently <a href="/wiki/Settler" title="Settler">settled</a> regions, present-day Turkey was home to important <a href="/wiki/Neolithic" title="Neolithic">Neolithic</a> sites like <a href="/wiki/G%C3%B6bekli_Tepe" title="Göbekli Tepe">Göbekli Tepe</a>, and was inhabited by <a href="/wiki/Civilization" title="Civilization">ancient civilisations</a> including the <a href="/wiki/Hattians" title="Hattians">Hattians</a>, <a href="/wiki/Hittites" title="Hittites">Hittites</a>, <a href="/wiki/Anatolian_peoples" title="Anatolian peoples">Anatolian peoples</a>, <a href="/wiki/Mycenaean_Greece" title="Mycenaean Greece">Mycenaean Greeks</a>, <a href="/wiki/Persians" title="Persians">Persians</a> and others.<sup id="cite_ref-Howard2_12-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Howard2-12">&#91;12&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-SteadmanMcMahon20112_13-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-SteadmanMcMahon20112-13">&#91;13&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-MET_14-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-MET-14">&#91;14&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-15" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-15">&#91;15&#93;</a></sup> Following the conquests of <a href="/wiki/Alexander_the_Great" title="Alexander the Great">Alexander the Great</a> which started the <a href="/wiki/Hellenistic_period" title="Hellenistic period">Hellenistic period</a>, most of the <a href="/wiki/Ancient_regions_of_Anatolia" title="Ancient regions of Anatolia">ancient regions</a> were culturally <a href="/wiki/Hellenization" title="Hellenization">Hellenised</a>, and this continued during the <a href="/wiki/Byzantine_Empire" title="Byzantine Empire">Byzantine era</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-SteadmanMcMahon20112_13-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-SteadmanMcMahon20112-13">&#91;13&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-FreedmanMyers20002_16-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FreedmanMyers20002-16">&#91;16&#93;</a></sup> The <a href="/wiki/Seljuk_Empire" title="Seljuk Empire">Seljuk Turks</a> began migrating in the 11th century, and the <a href="/wiki/Sultanate_of_Rum" title="Sultanate of Rum">Sultanate of Rum</a> ruled Anatolia until the <a href="/wiki/Mongol_invasions_of_Anatolia" title="Mongol invasions of Anatolia">Mongol invasion</a> in 1243, when it disintegrated into small <a href="/wiki/Anatolian_beyliks" title="Anatolian beyliks">Turkish principalities</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-mfk&amp;gl2_17-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-mfk&amp;gl2-17">&#91;17&#93;</a></sup> Beginning in the late 13th century, the <a href="/wiki/Ottoman_dynasty" title="Ottoman dynasty">Ottomans</a> <a href="/wiki/Rise_of_the_Ottoman_Empire" title="Rise of the Ottoman Empire">united the principalities and conquered the Balkans</a>, and the <a href="/wiki/Turkification" title="Turkification">Turkification</a> of Anatolia increased during the <a href="/wiki/Ottoman_Empire" title="Ottoman Empire">Ottoman period</a>. After <a href="/wiki/Mehmed_II" title="Mehmed II">Mehmed II</a> <a href="/wiki/Fall_of_Constantinople" title="Fall of Constantinople">conquered</a> <a href="/wiki/Constantinople" title="Constantinople">Constantinople</a> (now Istanbul) in 1453, Ottoman expansion continued under <a href="/wiki/Selim_I" title="Selim I">Selim I</a>. During the reign of <a href="/wiki/Suleiman_the_Magnificent" title="Suleiman the Magnificent">Suleiman the Magnificent</a>, the Ottoman Empire became a <a href="/wiki/Transformation_of_the_Ottoman_Empire" title="Transformation of the Ottoman Empire">global power</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-Howard2_12-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Howard2-12">&#91;12&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-masters_18-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-masters-18">&#91;18&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-19" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-19">&#91;19&#93;</a></sup> From the late 18th century onwards, the <a href="/wiki/Decline_and_modernization_of_the_Ottoman_Empire" title="Decline and modernization of the Ottoman Empire">empire's power declined</a> with a gradual loss of territories.<sup id="cite_ref-20" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-20">&#91;20&#93;</a></sup> <a href="/wiki/Mahmud_II" title="Mahmud II">Mahmud II</a> started a <a href="/wiki/Tanzimat" title="Tanzimat">period of modernisation</a> in the early 19th century.<sup id="cite_ref-21" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-21">&#91;21&#93;</a></sup> The <a href="/wiki/Young_Turk_Revolution" title="Young Turk Revolution">Young Turk Revolution</a> of 1908 restricted the authority of the Sultan and <a href="/wiki/Second_Constitutional_Era" title="Second Constitutional Era">restored</a> the <a href="/wiki/Ottoman_Parliament" class="mw-redirect" title="Ottoman Parliament">Ottoman Parliament</a> after a 30-year suspension, ushering the empire into a <a href="/wiki/List_of_political_parties_in_the_Ottoman_Empire" title="List of political parties in the Ottoman Empire">multi-party period</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-22" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-22">&#91;22&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-23" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-23">&#91;23&#93;</a></sup> The <a href="/wiki/Three_Pashas" title="Three Pashas">Three Pashas</a> took control with the <a href="/wiki/1913_Ottoman_coup_d%27%C3%A9tat" title="1913 Ottoman coup d&#39;état">1913 coup d'état</a>, and <a href="/wiki/Ottoman_entry_into_World_War_I" title="Ottoman entry into World War I">entered World War I</a> as one of the <a href="/wiki/Central_Powers" title="Central Powers">Central Powers</a> in 1914. During the war, the Ottoman government committed <a href="/wiki/Late_Ottoman_genocides" title="Late Ottoman genocides">genocides</a> against its <a href="/wiki/Armenian_genocide" title="Armenian genocide">Armenian</a>, <a href="/wiki/Greek_genocide" title="Greek genocide">Greek</a> and <a href="/wiki/Assyrian_genocide" class="mw-redirect" title="Assyrian genocide">Assyrian</a> subjects.<sup id="cite_ref-Tatz_24-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Tatz-24">&#91;24&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-SchallerZimmerer_25-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-SchallerZimmerer-25">&#91;25&#93;</a></sup> After its defeat in the war, the Ottoman Empire was <a href="/wiki/Partition_of_the_Ottoman_Empire" title="Partition of the Ottoman Empire">partitioned</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-26" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-26">&#91;26&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>The <a href="/wiki/Turkish_War_of_Independence" title="Turkish War of Independence">Turkish War of Independence</a> against the occupying <a href="/wiki/Allies_of_World_War_I" title="Allies of World War I">Allied Powers</a> resulted in the <a href="/wiki/Abolition_of_the_Ottoman_sultanate" title="Abolition of the Ottoman sultanate">abolition of the Sultanate</a> on 1 November 1922, the signing of the <a href="/wiki/Treaty_of_Lausanne" title="Treaty of Lausanne">Treaty of Lausanne</a> (which superseded the <a href="/wiki/Treaty_of_S%C3%A8vres" title="Treaty of Sèvres">Treaty of Sèvres</a>) on 24 July 1923 and the proclamation of the Republic on 29 October 1923. With the <a href="/wiki/Atat%C3%BCrk%27s_Reforms" class="mw-redirect" title="Atatürk&#39;s Reforms">reforms</a> initiated by the country's first president, <a href="/wiki/Mustafa_Kemal_Atat%C3%BCrk" title="Mustafa Kemal Atatürk">Mustafa Kemal Atatürk</a>, Turkey became a <a href="/wiki/Secular_state" title="Secular state">secular</a>, <a href="/wiki/Unitary_state" title="Unitary state">unitary</a> and <a href="/wiki/Parliamentary_republic" title="Parliamentary republic">parliamentary republic</a>. Turkey <a href="/wiki/Second_Cairo_Conference" title="Second Cairo Conference">remained neutral</a> during most of <a href="/wiki/World_War_II" title="World War II">World War II</a>, but entered the closing stages of the war on the side of the <a href="/wiki/Allies_of_World_War_II" title="Allies of World War II">Allies</a>. Turkey played a prominent role in the <a href="/wiki/Korean_War" title="Korean War">Korean War</a> and joined <a href="/wiki/Turkey_in_NATO" title="Turkey in NATO">NATO</a> in 1952. During the <a href="/wiki/Cold_War" title="Cold War">Cold War</a> years, the country endured two military <a href="/wiki/Coup" class="mw-redirect" title="Coup">coups</a> in <a href="/wiki/1960_Turkish_coup_d%27%C3%A9tat" title="1960 Turkish coup d&#39;état">1960</a> and <a href="/wiki/1980_Turkish_coup_d%27%C3%A9tat" title="1980 Turkish coup d&#39;état">1980</a>, and a period of economic and political turmoil in the 1970s. The economy was liberalised in the 1980s, leading to stronger <a href="/wiki/Economic_growth" title="Economic growth">economic growth</a> and political stability. Since <a href="/wiki/2002_Turkish_general_election" title="2002 Turkish general election">2002</a>, the country's political system has been dominated by the <a href="/wiki/Justice_and_Development_Party_(Turkey)" title="Justice and Development Party (Turkey)">AKP</a> and its leader <a href="/wiki/Recep_Tayyip_Erdo%C4%9Fan" title="Recep Tayyip Erdoğan">Recep Tayyip Erdoğan</a>, under whom a decade of rapid growth in <a href="/wiki/Nominal_GDP" class="mw-redirect" title="Nominal GDP">nominal GDP</a> took place until 2013,<sup id="cite_ref-countryeconomy-2013_27-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-countryeconomy-2013-27">&#91;27&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-IMF-2002-2023_28-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-IMF-2002-2023-28">&#91;28&#93;</a></sup> which was followed by a period of <a href="/wiki/Recession" title="Recession">recession</a> and <a href="/wiki/Economic_stagnation" title="Economic stagnation">stagnation</a> between 2013 and 2020,<sup id="cite_ref-IMF-2002-2023_28-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-IMF-2002-2023-28">&#91;28&#93;</a></sup> and high <a href="/wiki/Inflation" title="Inflation">inflation</a> as of 2023.<sup id="cite_ref-29" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-29">&#91;29&#93;</a></sup> The AKP government's initial economic achievements, which were financed through <a href="/wiki/Privatization_Board_of_Turkey" title="Privatization Board of Turkey">privatization</a> revenues and <a href="/wiki/National_debt_of_Turkey" title="National debt of Turkey">loans</a>, were overshadowed by <a href="/wiki/Democratic_backsliding" title="Democratic backsliding">democratic backsliding</a> and an erosion in the <a href="/wiki/Separation_of_powers" title="Separation of powers">separation of powers</a> and <a href="/wiki/Civil_liberties" title="Civil liberties">civil liberties</a>, which gained momentum after the <a href="/wiki/Parliamentary_republic" title="Parliamentary republic">parliamentary republic</a> was replaced by an <a href="/wiki/Executive_president" title="Executive president">executive</a> <a href="/wiki/Presidential_system" title="Presidential system">presidential system</a> with a <a href="/wiki/2017_Turkish_constitutional_referendum" title="2017 Turkish constitutional referendum">referendum in 2017</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-Oder_2021_pp._473–500_30-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Oder_2021_pp._473–500-30">&#91;30&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-31" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-31">&#91;31&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>Turkey is a <a href="/wiki/Regional_power" title="Regional power">regional power</a> with a geopolitically strategic location.<sup id="cite_ref-32" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-32">&#91;32&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-giga-hamburg.de1_33-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-giga-hamburg.de1-33">&#91;33&#93;</a></sup> The <a href="/wiki/Economy_of_Turkey" title="Economy of Turkey">economy</a> of Turkey, which is a founding member of the <a href="/wiki/OECD" title="OECD">OECD</a> and <a href="/wiki/G20" title="G20">G20</a>, is classified among the <a href="/wiki/Emerging_7" class="mw-redirect" title="Emerging 7">E7</a>, <a href="/wiki/Emerging_and_growth-leading_economies" title="Emerging and growth-leading economies">EAGLEs</a> and <a href="/wiki/Newly_industrialized_country" title="Newly industrialized country">NICs</a>, and currently ranks <a href="/wiki/List_of_countries_by_GDP_(nominal)" title="List of countries by GDP (nominal)">twentieth-largest in the world</a> by nominal GDP and <a href="/wiki/List_of_countries_by_GDP_(PPP)" title="List of countries by GDP (PPP)">eleventh-largest</a> by <a href="/wiki/Purchasing_power_parity" title="Purchasing power parity">PPP</a>. Turkey is a charter member of the <a href="/wiki/United_Nations" title="United Nations">United Nations</a>, the <a href="/wiki/International_Monetary_Fund" title="International Monetary Fund">IMF</a> and the <a href="/wiki/World_Bank" title="World Bank">World Bank</a>; a founding member of the <a href="/wiki/Organization_for_Security_and_Co-operation_in_Europe" title="Organization for Security and Co-operation in Europe">OSCE</a>, <a href="/wiki/Organisation_of_Islamic_Cooperation" title="Organisation of Islamic Cooperation">OIC</a>, <a href="/wiki/Organization_of_the_Black_Sea_Economic_Cooperation" title="Organization of the Black Sea Economic Cooperation">BSEC</a>, <a href="/wiki/Economic_Cooperation_Organization" title="Economic Cooperation Organization">ECO</a>, <a href="/wiki/MIKTA" title="MIKTA">MIKTA</a>, <a href="/wiki/International_Organization_of_Turkic_Culture" title="International Organization of Turkic Culture">TURKSOY</a> and <a href="/wiki/Organization_of_Turkic_States" title="Organization of Turkic States">OTS</a>; and an early member of <a href="/wiki/NATO" title="NATO">NATO</a>. After becoming <a href="/wiki/Member_states_of_the_Council_of_Europe" title="Member states of the Council of Europe">one of the early members</a> of the <a href="/wiki/Council_of_Europe" title="Council of Europe">Council of Europe</a> in 1950, Turkey became an <a href="/wiki/Ankara_Agreement" title="Ankara Agreement">associate member</a> of the <a href="/wiki/European_Economic_Community" title="European Economic Community">EEC</a> in 1963, joined the <a href="/wiki/European_Union_Customs_Union" title="European Union Customs Union">EU Customs Union</a> in 1995, and started <a href="/wiki/Accession_of_Turkey_to_the_European_Union" title="Accession of Turkey to the European Union">accession negotiations</a> with the <a href="/wiki/European_Union" title="European Union">European Union</a> in 2005. Turkey has a rich cultural legacy shaped by centuries of history and the influence of the various peoples that have inhabited its territory over several millennia; it is home to <a href="/wiki/List_of_World_Heritage_Sites_in_Turkey" title="List of World Heritage Sites in Turkey">19 UNESCO World Heritage Sites</a> and is <a href="/wiki/World_Tourism_rankings" title="World Tourism rankings">among the most visited</a> countries in the world.
</p>
<meta property="mw:PageProp/toc" />
<h2><span class="mw-headline" id="Name">Name</span></h2>
<link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1033289096"/><div role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">Main article: <a href="/wiki/Name_of_Turkey" title="Name of Turkey">Name of Turkey</a></div>
<p>The English name <i>Turkey</i> (from <a href="/wiki/Medieval_Latin" title="Medieval Latin">Medieval Latin</a> <span title="Latin-language text"><i lang="la">Turchia</i></span>/<span title="Latin-language text"><i lang="la">Turquia</i></span>)<sup id="cite_ref-arlen_34-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-arlen-34">&#91;34&#93;</a></sup> means "land of the Turks". <a href="/wiki/Middle_English" title="Middle English">Middle English</a> usage of <i><span title="Middle English (1100-1500)-language text"><i lang="enm">Turkye</i></span></i> is evidenced in an early work by <a href="/wiki/Chaucer" class="mw-redirect" title="Chaucer">Geoffrey Chaucer</a> called <i><a href="/wiki/The_Book_of_the_Duchess" title="The Book of the Duchess">The Book of the Duchess</a></i> (<abbr title="circa">c.</abbr><span style="white-space:nowrap;">&#8201;1369</span>). The phrase <i><span title="Middle English (1100-1500)-language text"><i lang="enm">land of Torke</i></span></i> is used in the 15th-century <a href="/wiki/The_Digby_Conversion_of_Saint_Paul" title="The Digby Conversion of Saint Paul">Digby Mysteries</a>. Later usages can be found in the <a href="/wiki/William_Dunbar" title="William Dunbar">William Dunbar poems</a>, the 16th century <span title="Latin-language text"><i lang="la"><a href="/wiki/Manipulus_Vocabulorum" title="Manipulus Vocabulorum">Manipulus Vocabulorum</a></i></span> (<i>Turkie</i>) and <a href="/wiki/Francis_Bacon" title="Francis Bacon">Francis Bacon</a>'s <span title="Latin-language text"><i lang="la">Sylva Sylvarum</i></span> (<i>Turky</i>). The modern spelling <i>Turkey</i> dates back to at least 1719.<sup id="cite_ref-35" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-35">&#91;35&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>The name <i>Turkey</i> appeared in the Western sources after the <a href="/wiki/Crusades" title="Crusades">Crusades</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-cevdet_36-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-cevdet-36">&#91;36&#93;</a></sup> In the 14th-century <a href="/wiki/Arabic_literature" title="Arabic literature">Arabic</a> sources, <i>Turkiyya</i> is usually contrasted with <i>Turkmaniyya</i> (<a href="/wiki/Turkomania_(disambiguation)" class="mw-disambig" title="Turkomania (disambiguation)">Turkomania</a>), probably to be understood as <a href="/wiki/Oghuz_Turks" title="Oghuz Turks">Oghuz</a> in a broad sense.<sup id="cite_ref-37" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-37">&#91;37&#93;</a></sup> In the 1330s, <a href="/wiki/Ibn_Battuta" title="Ibn Battuta">Ibn Battuta</a> defined the region as <i><span title="Arabic-language text"><i lang="ar-Latn">Barr al-Turkiyya al-ma'ruf bi-bilad al-Rûm</i></span><span class="lang-comment" style="font-style: normal; display: none; color: #33aa33; margin-left: 0.3em;">code: ara promoted to code: ar </span></i> ("the Turkish land known as the lands of <a href="/wiki/Sultanate_of_Rum" title="Sultanate of Rum">Rûm</a>").<sup id="cite_ref-38" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-38">&#91;38&#93;</a></sup> The disintegration of the country after <a href="/wiki/World_War_I" title="World War I">World War I</a> revived <a href="/wiki/Turkish_nationalism" title="Turkish nationalism">Turkish nationalism</a>, and the <i><span title="Turkish-language text"><i lang="tr">Türkler için Türkiye</i></span><span class="lang-comment" style="font-style: normal; display: none; color: #33aa33; margin-left: 0.3em;">code: tur promoted to code: tr </span></i> ("Turkey for the Turks") sentiment rose up. With the <a href="/wiki/Treaty_of_Alexandropol" title="Treaty of Alexandropol">Treaty of Alexandropol</a> signed by the <a href="/wiki/Government_of_the_Grand_National_Assembly" title="Government of the Grand National Assembly">Government of the Grand National Assembly</a> with <a href="/wiki/First_Armenian_Republic" class="mw-redirect" title="First Armenian Republic">Armenia</a>, the name <i>Türkiye</i> entered international documents for the first time. In the treaty signed with <a href="/wiki/Kingdom_of_Afghanistan" title="Kingdom of Afghanistan">Afghanistan</a>, the expression <i>Devlet-i Âliyye-i Türkiyye</i> ("Sublime Turkish State") was used, likened to the Ottoman Empire's <a href="/wiki/Ottoman_Empire#Name" title="Ottoman Empire">name</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-cevdet_36-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-cevdet-36">&#91;36&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<h3><span class="mw-headline" id="Official_name_change">Official name change</span></h3>
<p>In January 2020, the Turkish Exporters' Assembly — the umbrella organisation of Turkish exports — announced that it would use "Made in Türkiye" on all of its labels, in a bid to standardise the branding and identity of Turkish businesses on the international stage, using the term 'Türkiye' across all languages around the world.<sup id="cite_ref-:5_39-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-:5-39">&#91;39&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>In December 2021, President <a href="/wiki/Recep_Tayyip_Erdo%C4%9Fan" title="Recep Tayyip Erdoğan">Recep Tayyip Erdoğan</a> issued a circular, calling for exports to be labelled "Made in Türkiye". The circular also stated that in relation to other governmental communications, the "necessary sensitivity will be shown on the use of the phrase 'Türkiye' instead of phrases such as 'Turkey', 'Türkei', 'Turquie' etc."<sup id="cite_ref-40" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-40">&#91;40&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-41" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-41">&#91;41&#93;</a></sup> The reason given in the circular for preferring <i>Türkiye</i> was that it "represents and expresses the culture, civilisation, and values of the Turkish nation in the best way". According to Turkish state broadcaster <a href="/wiki/TRT_World" title="TRT World">TRT World</a>, it was also to avoid a pejorative association with <a href="/wiki/Turkey_(bird)" title="Turkey (bird)">turkey, the bird</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-:5_39-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-:5-39">&#91;39&#93;</a></sup> It was reported in January 2022 that the government planned to register <i>Türkiye</i> with the <a href="/wiki/United_Nations" title="United Nations">United Nations</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-42" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-42">&#91;42&#93;</a></sup> Minister of Foreign Affairs <a href="/wiki/Mevl%C3%BCt_%C3%87avu%C5%9Fo%C4%9Flu" title="Mevlüt Çavuşoğlu">Mevlüt Çavuşoğlu</a> sent letters to the UN and other international organisations on 31 May 2022, requesting that they use <i>Türkiye</i>. The UN agreed and implemented the request immediately.<sup id="cite_ref-43" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-43">&#91;43&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-44" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-44">&#91;44&#93;</a></sup> The <a href="/wiki/United_States_Department_of_State" title="United States Department of State">United States Department of State</a> officially began using <i>Türkiye</i> in January 2023.<sup id="cite_ref-45" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-45">&#91;45&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<h2><span class="mw-headline" id="History">History</span></h2>
<link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1033289096"/><div role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">Main article: <a href="/wiki/History_of_Turkey" title="History of Turkey">History of Turkey</a></div>
<link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1033289096"/><div role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">See also: <a href="/wiki/History_of_Anatolia" title="History of Anatolia">History of Anatolia</a> and <a href="/wiki/History_of_Thrace" class="mw-redirect" title="History of Thrace">History of Thrace</a></div>
<h3><span class="mw-headline" id="Prehistory_of_Anatolia_and_Eastern_Thrace">Prehistory of Anatolia and Eastern Thrace</span></h3>
<link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1033289096"/><div role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">Main articles: <a href="/wiki/Prehistory_of_Anatolia" title="Prehistory of Anatolia">Prehistory of Anatolia</a> and <a href="/wiki/Prehistory_of_Southeastern_Europe" title="Prehistory of Southeastern Europe">Prehistory of Southeastern Europe</a></div>
<div class="thumb tleft"><div class="thumbinner" style="width:222px;"><a href="/wiki/File:G%C3%B6bekli_Tepe,_Urfa.jpg" class="image"><img alt="" src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/d5/G%C3%B6bekli_Tepe%2C_Urfa.jpg/220px-G%C3%B6bekli_Tepe%2C_Urfa.jpg" decoding="async" width="220" height="146" class="thumbimage" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/d5/G%C3%B6bekli_Tepe%2C_Urfa.jpg/330px-G%C3%B6bekli_Tepe%2C_Urfa.jpg 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/d5/G%C3%B6bekli_Tepe%2C_Urfa.jpg/440px-G%C3%B6bekli_Tepe%2C_Urfa.jpg 2x" data-file-width="4288" data-file-height="2848" /></a>  <div class="thumbcaption"><div class="magnify"><a href="/wiki/File:G%C3%B6bekli_Tepe,_Urfa.jpg" class="internal" title="Enlarge"></a></div>Some <a href="/wiki/Henge" title="Henge">henges</a> at <a href="/wiki/G%C3%B6bekli_Tepe" title="Göbekli Tepe">Göbekli Tepe</a> were erected as far back as <a href="/wiki/G%C3%B6bekli_Tepe#Layer_III" title="Göbekli Tepe">9600 BC</a>, predating those of <a href="/wiki/Stonehenge" title="Stonehenge">Stonehenge</a>, England, by over seven millennia.<sup id="cite_ref-ArchMag_46-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-ArchMag-46">&#91;46&#93;</a></sup></div></div></div>
<p>The <a href="/wiki/Anatolia" title="Anatolia">Anatolian peninsula</a>, comprising most of modern Turkey, is one of the oldest permanently settled regions in the world. Various <a href="/wiki/Ancient_Anatolians" class="mw-redirect" title="Ancient Anatolians">ancient Anatolian</a> populations have lived in <a href="/wiki/Anatolia" title="Anatolia">Anatolia</a>, from at least the <a href="/wiki/Neolithic" title="Neolithic">Neolithic</a> until the <a href="/wiki/Hellenistic_civilization" class="mw-redirect" title="Hellenistic civilization">Hellenistic period</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-SteadmanMcMahon20112_13-2" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-SteadmanMcMahon20112-13">&#91;13&#93;</a></sup> Many of these peoples spoke the <a href="/wiki/Anatolian_languages" title="Anatolian languages">Anatolian languages</a>, a branch of the larger <a href="/wiki/Indo-European_language_family" class="mw-redirect" title="Indo-European language family">Indo-European language family</a>:<sup id="cite_ref-UCLA_47-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-UCLA-47">&#91;47&#93;</a></sup> and, given the antiquity of the Indo-European <a href="/wiki/Hittite_language" title="Hittite language">Hittite</a> and <a href="/wiki/Luwian_language" title="Luwian language">Luwian</a> languages, some scholars have proposed <a href="/wiki/Anatolian_hypothesis" title="Anatolian hypothesis">Anatolia as the hypothetical centre from which the Indo-European languages radiated</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-AnatoliaIndoEuropean_48-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-AnatoliaIndoEuropean-48">&#91;48&#93;</a></sup> The European part of Turkey, called <a href="/wiki/Eastern_Thrace" class="mw-redirect" title="Eastern Thrace">Eastern Thrace</a>, has also been inhabited since at least forty thousand years ago, and is known to have been in the Neolithic era by about 6000 BC.<sup id="cite_ref-MET_14-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-MET-14">&#91;14&#93;</a></sup> The <a href="/wiki/Neolithic_Revolution" title="Neolithic Revolution">spread of agriculture</a> from the Middle East to Europe was strongly correlated with the <a href="/wiki/Pre-modern_human_migration" title="Pre-modern human migration">migration</a> of <a href="/wiki/Early_European_Farmers" title="Early European Farmers">early farmers from Anatolia</a> about 9,000 years ago, and was not just a cultural exchange.<sup id="cite_ref-49" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-49">&#91;49&#93;</a></sup> Anatolian Neolithic farmers derived a significant portion of their ancestry from the <a href="/wiki/Anatolian_hunter-gatherers" title="Anatolian hunter-gatherers">Anatolian hunter-gatherers</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-50" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-50">&#91;50&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p><a href="/wiki/G%C3%B6bekli_Tepe" title="Göbekli Tepe">Göbekli Tepe</a> is the site of the oldest known man-made religious structure, a temple dating to circa 10,000 BC,<sup id="cite_ref-ArchMag_46-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-ArchMag-46">&#91;46&#93;</a></sup> while <a href="/wiki/%C3%87atalh%C3%B6y%C3%BCk" title="Çatalhöyük">Çatalhöyük</a> is a very large Neolithic and <a href="/wiki/Chalcolithic" title="Chalcolithic">Chalcolithic</a> settlement in southern Anatolia, which existed from approximately 7500 BC to 5700 BC. It is the largest and best-preserved Neolithic site found to date and is a <a href="/wiki/UNESCO_World_Heritage_Site" class="mw-redirect" title="UNESCO World Heritage Site">UNESCO World Heritage Site</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-51" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-51">&#91;51&#93;</a></sup> <a href="/wiki/Neval%C4%B1_%C3%87ori" title="Nevalı Çori">Nevalı Çori</a> was an early <a href="/wiki/Neolithic" title="Neolithic">Neolithic</a> settlement on the middle Euphrates, in <a href="/wiki/%C5%9Eanl%C4%B1urfa" class="mw-redirect" title="Şanlıurfa">Şanlıurfa</a>. The <a href="/wiki/Urfa_Man" title="Urfa Man">Urfa Man</a> statue is dated c. 9000 BC, to the period of the <a href="/wiki/Pre-Pottery_Neolithic" title="Pre-Pottery Neolithic">Pre-Pottery Neolithic</a>, and is defined as "the oldest known naturalistic life-sized sculpture of a human".<sup id="cite_ref-RJC_52-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-RJC-52">&#91;52&#93;</a></sup> It is considered to be contemporaneous with <a href="/wiki/G%C3%B6bekli_Tepe" title="Göbekli Tepe">Göbekli Tepe</a> and the nearby archaeological sites. The settlement of <a href="/wiki/Troy" title="Troy">Troy</a> started in the Neolithic Age and continued into the <a href="/wiki/Iron_Age" title="Iron Age">Iron Age</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-53" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-53">&#91;53&#93;</a></sup>
</p>

class="trow"><div class="tsingle" style="width:222px;max-width:222px"><div class="thumbimage"><a href="/wiki/File:Aizanoi_Zeus_temple_2120.jpg" class="image"><img alt="" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/44/Aizanoi_Zeus_temple_2120.jpg/330px-Aizanoi_Zeus_temple_2120.jpg 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/44/Aizanoi_Zeus_temple_2120.jpg/440px-Aizanoi_Zeus_temple_2120.jpg 2x" data-file-width="1600" data-file-height="1065" /></a></div><div class="thumbcaption">The <a href="/wiki/Aizanoi#Temple_of_Zeus" title="Aizanoi">Temple of Zeus</a> in the ancient city of <a href="/wiki/Aizanoi" title="Aizanoi">Aizanoi</a> in <a href="/wiki/Phrygia" title="Phrygia">Phrygia</a>.</div></div></div></div></div>
<p>The earliest recorded inhabitants of Anatolia were the <a href="/wiki/Hattians" title="Hattians">Hattians</a> and <a href="/wiki/Hurrians" title="Hurrians">Hurrians</a>, non-Indo-European peoples who inhabited central and eastern Anatolia, respectively, as early as c. 2300 BC. Indo-European <a href="/wiki/Hittites" title="Hittites">Hittites</a> came to Anatolia and gradually absorbed the Hattians and Hurrians c. 2000–1700 BC. The first major empire in the area was founded by the Hittites, from the 18th through the 13th century BC. The <a href="/wiki/Assyria" title="Assyria">Assyrians</a> conquered and settled parts of southeastern Turkey as early as 1950 BC until the year 612 BC,<sup id="cite_ref-54" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-54">&#91;54&#93;</a></sup> although they <a href="/wiki/Assyrian_continuity" title="Assyrian continuity">have remained a minority</a> in the region, namely in <a href="/wiki/Hakk%C3%A2ri_Province" title="Hakkâri Province">Hakkari</a>, <a href="/wiki/%C5%9E%C4%B1rnak_Province" title="Şırnak Province">Şırnak</a> and <a href="/wiki/Mardin_province" class="mw-redirect" title="Mardin province">Mardin</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-55" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-55">&#91;55&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p><a href="/wiki/Urartu" title="Urartu">Urartu</a> re-emerged in Assyrian inscriptions in the 9th century BC as a powerful northern rival of Assyria.<sup id="cite_ref-56" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-56">&#91;56&#93;</a></sup> Following the collapse of the Hittite empire c. 1180 BC, the <a href="/wiki/Phrygia" title="Phrygia">Phrygians</a>, an Indo-European people, achieved ascendancy in Anatolia until their kingdom was destroyed by the <a href="/wiki/Cimmerians" title="Cimmerians">Cimmerians</a> in the 7th century BC.<sup id="cite_ref-TroyHittiteEmpirePhrygians_57-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-TroyHittiteEmpirePhrygians-57">&#91;57&#93;</a></sup> Starting from 714 BC, Urartu shared the same fate and dissolved in 590 BC,<sup id="cite_ref-58" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-58">&#91;58&#93;</a></sup> when it was conquered by the <a href="/wiki/Medes" title="Medes">Medes</a>. The most powerful of Phrygia's successor states were <a href="/wiki/Lydia" title="Lydia">Lydia</a>, <a href="/wiki/Caria" title="Caria">Caria</a> and <a href="/wiki/Lycia" title="Lycia">Lycia</a>.
</p><p><a href="/wiki/Sardis" title="Sardis">Sardis</a> was an ancient city at the location of modern Sart in Western Turkey. The city served as the capital of the ancient kingdom of <a href="/wiki/Lydia" title="Lydia">Lydia</a>. As one of the <a href="/wiki/Seven_churches_of_Asia" title="Seven churches of Asia">seven churches of Asia</a>, it was addressed in the <a href="/wiki/Book_of_Revelation" title="Book of Revelation">Book of Revelation</a> in the <a href="/wiki/New_Testament" title="New Testament">New Testament</a>,<sup id="cite_ref-59" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-59">&#91;59&#93;</a></sup> The <a href="/wiki/Lydia" title="Lydia">Lydian Lion</a> coins were made of <a href="/wiki/Electrum" title="Electrum">electrum</a>, a naturally occurring alloy of gold and silver but of variable precious metal value. During the reign of King <a href="/wiki/Croesus" title="Croesus">Croesus</a> that the <a href="/wiki/Metallurgist" class="mw-redirect" title="Metallurgist">metallurgists</a> of Sardis discovered the secret of separating <a href="/wiki/Gold" title="Gold">gold</a> from <a href="/wiki/Silver" title="Silver">silver</a>, thereby producing both metals of a purity never known before.<sup id="cite_ref-60" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-60">&#91;60&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<h3><span class="mw-headline" id="Antiquity">Antiquity</span></h3>
<link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1033289096"/><div role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">Main articles: <a href="/wiki/Classical_Anatolia" title="Classical Anatolia">Classical Anatolia</a> and <a href="/wiki/Hellenistic_period" title="Hellenistic period">Hellenistic period</a></div>
<div class="thumb tleft"><div class="thumbinner" style="width:222px;"><a href="/wiki/File:The_Bath-Gymnasium_complex_at_Sardis,_late_2nd_-_early_3rd_century_AD,_Sardis,_Turkey_(17098680002).jpg" class="image"><img alt="" src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/e/e5/The_Bath-Gymnasium_complex_at_Sardis%2C_late_2nd_-_early_3rd_century_AD%2C_Sardis%2C_Turkey_%2817098680002%29.jpg/220px-The_Bath-Gymnasium_complex_at_Sardis%2C_late_2nd_-_early_3rd_century_AD%2C_Sardis%2C_Turkey_%2817098680002%29.jpg" decoding="async" width="220" height="146" class="thumbimage" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/e/e5/The_Bath-Gymnasium_complex_at_Sardis%2C_late_2nd_-_early_3rd_century_AD%2C_Sardis%2C_Turkey_%2817098680002%29.jpg/330px-The_Bath-Gymnasium_complex_at_Sardis%2C_late_2nd_-_early_3rd_century_AD%2C_Sardis%2C_Turkey_%2817098680002%29.jpg 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/e/e5/The_Bath-Gymnasium_complex_at_Sardis%2C_late_2nd_-_early_3rd_century_AD%2C_Sardis%2C_Turkey_%2817098680002%29.jpg/440px-The_Bath-Gymnasium_complex_at_Sardis%2C_late_2nd_-_early_3rd_century_AD%2C_Sardis%2C_Turkey_%2817098680002%29.jpg 2x" data-file-width="4903" data-file-height="3252" /></a>  <div class="thumbcaption"><div class="magnify"><a href="/wiki/File:The_Bath-Gymnasium_complex_at_Sardis,_late_2nd_-_early_3rd_century_AD,_Sardis,_Turkey_(17098680002).jpg" class="internal" title="Enlarge"></a></div>The gymnasium complex in <a href="/wiki/Sardis" title="Sardis">Sardis</a>, the capital of <a href="/wiki/Lydia" title="Lydia">Lydia</a>.</div></div></div>
<p>Starting around 1200 BC, the coast of Anatolia was heavily settled by <a href="/wiki/Aeolians" title="Aeolians">Aeolian</a> and <a href="/wiki/Ionians" title="Ionians">Ionian</a> <a href="/wiki/Ancient_Greece" title="Ancient Greece">Greeks</a>. Numerous important <a href="/wiki/Polis" title="Polis">cities</a> were founded by these colonists, such as <a href="/wiki/Miletus" title="Miletus">Miletus</a>, <a href="/wiki/Ephesus" title="Ephesus">Ephesus</a>, <a href="/wiki/Halicarnassus" title="Halicarnassus">Halicarnassus</a>, <a href="/wiki/Pergamon" title="Pergamon">Pergamon</a>, <a href="/wiki/Aphrodisias" title="Aphrodisias">Aphrodisias</a>, <a href="/wiki/Smyrna" title="Smyrna">Smyrna</a> (now <a href="/wiki/%C4%B0zmir" title="İzmir">İzmir</a>) and <a href="/wiki/Byzantium" title="Byzantium">Byzantium</a> (now <a href="/wiki/Istanbul" title="Istanbul">Istanbul</a>), the latter founded by <a href="/wiki/Greeks" title="Greeks">Greek</a> colonists from <a href="/wiki/Megara" title="Megara">Megara</a> in c. <a href="/wiki/Byzantium#History" title="Byzantium">667 BC</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-61" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-61">&#91;61&#93;</a></sup> Some of the most prominent <a href="/wiki/Pre-Socratic_philosophy" title="Pre-Socratic philosophy">pre-Socratic philosophers</a> lived in the city of <a href="/wiki/Miletus" title="Miletus">Miletus</a>. <a href="/wiki/Thales_of_Miletus" title="Thales of Miletus">Thales of Miletus</a> (c. 624 BC – c. 546 BC) is regarded as the first philosopher in the <a href="/wiki/Greek_philosophy" class="mw-redirect" title="Greek philosophy">Greek tradition</a>,<sup id="cite_ref-62" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-62">&#91;62&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-CPM_63-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-CPM-63">&#91;63&#93;</a></sup> and is also historically recognized as the first individual known to have engaged in <a href="/wiki/History_of_science#Pre-socratics" title="History of science">scientific philosophy</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-64" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-64">&#91;64&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-books.google.com_65-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-books.google.com-65">&#91;65&#93;</a></sup> Thales is often referred to as the "Father of Science".<sup id="cite_ref-66" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-66">&#91;66&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-67" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-67">&#91;67&#93;</a></sup> In Miletus, he was followed by two other significant pre-Socratic philosophers, <a href="/wiki/Anaximander" title="Anaximander">Anaximander</a> (c. 610 BC – c. 546 BC) and <a href="/wiki/Anaximenes_of_Miletus" title="Anaximenes of Miletus">Anaximenes</a> (c. 585 BC – c. 525 BC) (known collectively, to modern scholars, as the <a href="/wiki/Milesian_school" class="mw-redirect" title="Milesian school">Milesian school</a>). For several centuries prior to the <a href="/wiki/Greco-Persian_Wars" title="Greco-Persian Wars">first Persian invasion of Greece</a>, perhaps the greatest and wealthiest city of the Greek world was Miletus, which founded more colonies than any other Greek city,<sup id="cite_ref-68" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-68">&#91;68&#93;</a></sup> particularly in the <a href="/wiki/Black_Sea" title="Black Sea">Black Sea</a> region. <a href="/wiki/Diogenes_the_Cynic" class="mw-redirect" title="Diogenes the Cynic">Diogenes the Cynic</a> was one of the founders of the <a href="/wiki/Cynicism_(philosophy)" title="Cynicism (philosophy)">Cynic</a> philosophy, born in one of the <a href="/wiki/Ionians" title="Ionians">Ionian</a> colonies, <a href="/wiki/Sinop,_Turkey" title="Sinop, Turkey">Sinope</a>, on the Black Sea coast of Anatolia, in 412 BC.<sup id="cite_ref-VoiceWilder_69-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-VoiceWilder-69">&#91;69&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1096954695/mw-parser-output/.tmulti"/><div class="thumb tmulti tright"><div class="thumbinner multiimageinner" style="width:348px;max-width:348px"><div class="trow"><div class="tsingle" style="width:162px;max-width:162px"><div class="thumbimage"><a href="/wiki/File:Didyma_m%C3%A9dusa_2009_04_28.jpg" class="image"><img alt="" src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/06/Didyma_m%C3%A9dusa_2009_04_28.jpg/160px-Didyma_m%C3%A9dusa_2009_04_28.jpg" decoding="async" width="160" height="120" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/06/Didyma_m%C3%A9dusa_2009_04_28.jpg/240px-Didyma_m%C3%A9dusa_2009_04_28.jpg 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/06/Didyma_m%C3%A9dusa_2009_04_28.jpg/320px-Didyma_m%C3%A9dusa_2009_04_28.jpg 2x" data-file-width="3264" data-file-height="2448" /></a></div></div><div class="tsingle" style="width:182px;max-width:182px"><div class="thumbimage"><a href="/wiki/File:Didymaion_front_AvL.JPG" class="image"><img alt="" src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/54/Didymaion_front_AvL.JPG/180px-Didymaion_front_AvL.JPG" decoding="async" width="180" height="120" //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/54/Didymaion_front_AvL.JPG/360px-Didymaion_front_AvL.JPG 2x" data-file-width="4896" data-file-height="3264" /></a></div></div></div><div class="trow" style="display:flex"><div class="thumbcaption">Head of <a href="/wiki/Medusa" title="Medusa">Medusa</a> (left) in <a href="/wiki/Didyma" title="Didyma">Didyma</a> (<a href="/wiki/Ancient_Greek_language" class="mw-redirect" title="Ancient Greek language">Ancient Greek</a>: <span lang="grc">Δίδυμα</span>, meaning "Twins"), home to the <i>Didymaion</i> which consists of two temples dedicated to the Olympian twins <a href="/wiki/Artemis" title="Artemis">Artemis</a> and <a href="/wiki/Apollo" title="Apollo">Apollo</a> (right). The <a href="/wiki/Sanctuary" title="Sanctuary">sanctuary</a>, near the ancient city of <a href="/wiki/Miletus" title="Miletus">Miletus</a>, was renowned in antiquity for its famed <a href="/wiki/Oracle#Oracle_at_Didyma" title="Oracle">oracle</a>.</div></div></div></div>
<p>The <a href="/wiki/Trojan_War" title="Trojan War">Trojan War</a> took place in the ancient city of <a href="/wiki/Troy" title="Troy">Troy</a>, between the <a href="/wiki/Troy" title="Troy">Trojans</a> and <a href="/wiki/Achaeans_(Homer)" title="Achaeans (Homer)">Achaeans</a> (<a href="/wiki/Mycenaean_Greece" title="Mycenaean Greece">Mycenaean Greeks</a>), after Prince <a href="/wiki/Paris_(mythology)" title="Paris (mythology)">Paris</a> of Troy took Queen <a href="/wiki/Helen_of_Troy" title="Helen of Troy">Helen</a> from her husband <a href="/wiki/Menelaus" title="Menelaus">Menelaus</a>, King of <a href="/wiki/Sparta" title="Sparta">Sparta</a>, the younger brother of <a href="/wiki/Agamemnon" title="Agamemnon">Agamemnon</a>, King of <a href="/wiki/Mycenae" title="Mycenae">Mycenae</a>, who led the Achaeans. The war is one of the most important events in ancient <a href="/wiki/Greek_mythology" title="Greek mythology">Greek mythology</a> and has been narrated through many works of <a href="/wiki/Ancient_Greek_literature" title="Ancient Greek literature">Greek literature</a>, most notably <a href="/wiki/Homer" title="Homer">Homer</a>'s <i><a href="/wiki/Iliad" title="Iliad">Iliad</a></i>. Whether there is any historical reality behind the Trojan War remains an open question. Those who believe that the stories of the Trojan War are derived from a specific historical conflict usually date it to the 12th or 11th century BC, often preferring the dates given by <a href="/wiki/Eratosthenes" title="Eratosthenes">Eratosthenes</a>, 1194–1184 BC, which roughly correspond to archaeological evidence of a catastrophic burning of <a href="/wiki/Troy_VII" class="mw-redirect" title="Troy VII">Troy VII</a>,<sup id="cite_ref-70" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-70">&#91;70&#93;</a></sup> and the <a href="/wiki/Late_Bronze_Age_collapse" title="Late Bronze Age collapse">Late Bronze Age collapse</a>.
</p><p>The first state that was called <a href="/wiki/Armenia" title="Armenia">Armenia</a> by the neighbouring peoples was the state of the <a href="/wiki/Armenians" title="Armenians">Armenian</a> <a href="/wiki/Orontid_dynasty" title="Orontid dynasty">Orontid dynasty</a>, which included parts of what is now eastern Turkey, beginning in the 6th century BC. In northwestern Turkey, the most significant tribal group in ancient <a href="/wiki/Thrace" title="Thrace">Thrace</a> was the <a href="/wiki/Odrysian_kingdom" title="Odrysian kingdom">Odyrisians</a>, founded by <a href="/wiki/Teres_I" title="Teres I">Teres I</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-LewisBoardman1994_71-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-LewisBoardman1994-71">&#91;71&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1096954695/mw-parser-output/.tmulti"/><div class="thumb tmulti tright"><div class="thumbinner multiimageinner" style="width:234px;max-width:234px"><div class="trow"><div class="tsingle" style="width:232px;max-width:232px"><div class="thumbimage"><a href="/wiki/File:Afrodisias_-_Sebasti%C3%B3n_-_Sebasteion.jpg" class="image"><img alt="" src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/54/Afrodisias_-_Sebasti%C3%B3n_-_Sebasteion.jpg/230px-Afrodisias_-_Sebasti%C3%B3n_-_Sebasteion.jpg" decoding="async" width="230" height="153" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/54/Afrodisias_-_Sebasti%C3%B3n_-_Sebasteion.jpg/345px-Afrodisias_-_Sebasti%C3%B3n_-_Sebasteion.jpg 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/54/Afrodisias_-_Sebasti%C3%B3n_-_Sebasteion.jpg/460px-Afrodisias_-_Sebasti%C3%B3n_-_Sebasteion.jpg 2x" data-file-width="3648" data-file-height="2432" /></a></div><div class="thumbcaption">The <a href="/wiki/Sebasteion" class="mw-redirect" title="Sebasteion">Sebasteion</a> of <a href="/wiki/Aphrodisias" title="Aphrodisias">Aphrodisias</a>, a city named after <a href="/wiki/Aphrodite" title="Aphrodite">Aphrodite</a>, the Greek goddess of beauty. In 2017, it was inscribed on the <a href="/wiki/UNESCO" title="UNESCO">UNESCO</a> <a href="/wiki/List_of_World_Heritage_Sites_in_Turkey" title="List of World Heritage Sites in Turkey">World Heritage Site</a> list.<sup id="cite_ref-72" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-72">&#91;72&#93;</a></sup></div></div></div><div class="trow"><div class="tsingle" style="width:232px;max-width:232px"><div class="thumbimage"><a href="/wiki/File:Ephesus_Celsus_Library_Fa%C3%A7ade.jpg" class="image"><img alt="" src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/84/Ephesus_Celsus_Library_Fa%C3%A7ade.jpg/230px-Ephesus_Celsus_Library_Fa%C3%A7ade.jpg" decoding="async" width="230" height="178" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/84/Ephesus_Celsus_Library_Fa%C3%A7ade.jpg/345px-Ephesus_Celsus_Library_Fa%C3%A7ade.jpg 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/84/Ephesus_Celsus_Library_Fa%C3%A7ade.jpg/460px-Ephesus_Celsus_Library_Fa%C3%A7ade.jpg 2x" data-file-width="9163" data-file-height="7100" /></a></div><div class="thumbcaption">The <a href="/wiki/Library_of_Celsus" title="Library of Celsus">Library of Celsus</a> in <a href="/wiki/Ephesus" title="Ephesus">Ephesus</a> was built by the <a href="/wiki/Roman_Empire" title="Roman Empire">Romans</a> in 114–117.<sup id="cite_ref-73" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-73">&#91;73&#93;</a></sup> The <a href="/wiki/Temple_of_Artemis" title="Temple of Artemis">Temple of Artemis</a> in Ephesus, built by king <a href="/wiki/Croesus" title="Croesus">Croesus</a> of <a href="/wiki/Lydia" title="Lydia">Lydia</a> in the 6th century BC, was one of the <a href="/wiki/Seven_Wonders_of_the_Ancient_World" title="Seven Wonders of the Ancient World">Seven Wonders of the Ancient World</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-74" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-74">&#91;74&#93;</a></sup></div></div></div></div></div>
<p>All of modern-day Turkey was conquered by the Persian <a href="/wiki/Achaemenid_Empire" title="Achaemenid Empire">Achaemenid Empire</a> during the 6th century BC.<sup id="cite_ref-A_companion_to_Ancient_Macedonia_75-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-A_companion_to_Ancient_Macedonia-75">&#91;75&#93;</a></sup> The <a href="/wiki/Greco-Persian_Wars" title="Greco-Persian Wars">Greco-Persian Wars</a> started when the Greek city states on the coast of Anatolia rebelled against Persian rule in 499 BC. Queen <a href="/wiki/Artemisia_I_of_Caria" title="Artemisia I of Caria">Artemisia I</a> of the ancient Greek <a href="/wiki/Polis" title="Polis">city-state</a> of <a href="/wiki/Halicarnassus" title="Halicarnassus">Halicarnassus</a>, which was then within the Achaemenid <a href="/wiki/Satrapy" class="mw-redirect" title="Satrapy">satrapy</a> of <a href="/wiki/Caria" title="Caria">Caria</a>, fought as an ally of <a href="/wiki/Xerxes_I" title="Xerxes I">Xerxes I</a>, King of Persia, against the independent Greek city-states during the <a href="/wiki/Second_Persian_invasion_of_Greece" title="Second Persian invasion of Greece">second Persian invasion of Greece</a> in 480 BC.<sup id="cite_ref-76" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-76">&#91;76&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-77" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-77">&#91;77&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>The territory of Turkey later fell to <a href="/wiki/Alexander_the_Great" title="Alexander the Great">Alexander the Great</a> in 334 BC,<sup id="cite_ref-PersiansInAsiaMinor_78-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-PersiansInAsiaMinor-78">&#91;78&#93;</a></sup> which led to increasing cultural homogeneity and <a href="/wiki/Hellenization" title="Hellenization">Hellenization</a> in the area.<sup id="cite_ref-SteadmanMcMahon20112_13-3" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-SteadmanMcMahon20112-13">&#91;13&#93;</a></sup> Following Alexander's death in 323 BC, Anatolia was subsequently divided into a number of small <a href="/wiki/Hellenistic_period" title="Hellenistic period">Hellenistic kingdoms</a>, all of which became part of the <a href="/wiki/Roman_Republic" title="Roman Republic">Roman Republic</a> by the mid-1st century BC.<sup id="cite_ref-AlexanderToRome_79-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-AlexanderToRome-79">&#91;79&#93;</a></sup> The process of Hellenization that began with Alexander's conquest accelerated under Roman rule, and by the early centuries of the <a href="/wiki/Christian_Era" class="mw-redirect" title="Christian Era">Christian Era</a>, the local <a href="/wiki/Anatolian_languages" title="Anatolian languages">Anatolian languages</a> and cultures had become extinct, being largely replaced by <a href="/wiki/Ancient_Greek_language" class="mw-redirect" title="Ancient Greek language">ancient Greek language</a> and culture.<sup id="cite_ref-FreedmanMyers20002_16-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FreedmanMyers20002-16">&#91;16&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-Hout2011_80-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Hout2011-80">&#91;80&#93;</a></sup> From the 1st century BC up to the 3rd century AD, large parts of modern-day Turkey were contested between the <a href="/wiki/Roman_Empire" title="Roman Empire">Romans</a> and neighbouring <a href="/wiki/Parthian_Empire" title="Parthian Empire">Parthians</a> through the frequent <a href="/wiki/Roman-Parthian_Wars" class="mw-redirect" title="Roman-Parthian Wars">Roman-Parthian Wars</a>.
</p><p><a href="/wiki/Galatia" title="Galatia">Galatia</a> was an ancient area in the highlands of central Anatolia inhabited by the <a href="/wiki/Celts" title="Celts">Celts</a>. The terms "Galatians" came to be used by the Greeks for the three Celtic peoples of Anatolia: the <a href="/wiki/Tectosages" title="Tectosages">Tectosages</a>, the <a href="/wiki/Trocmii" class="mw-redirect" title="Trocmii">Trocmii</a>, and the <a href="/wiki/Tolistobogii" title="Tolistobogii">Tolistobogii</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-OUP_81-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-OUP-81">&#91;81&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-82" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-82">&#91;82&#93;</a></sup> By the 1st century BC the Celts had become so <a href="/wiki/Hellenization" title="Hellenization">Hellenized</a> that some Greek writers called them <i>Hellenogalatai</i> (Ἑλληνογαλάται).<sup id="cite_ref-83" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-83">&#91;83&#93;</a></sup> Galatia was named after the <a href="/wiki/Gauls" title="Gauls">Gauls</a> from <a href="/wiki/Thrace" title="Thrace">Thrace</a> (cf. <a href="/wiki/Tylis" title="Tylis">Tylis</a>), who settled here and became a small transient foreign tribe in the 3rd century BC, following the supposed <a href="/wiki/Gallic_invasion_of_the_Balkans" class="mw-redirect" title="Gallic invasion of the Balkans">Gallic invasion of the Balkans</a> in 279 BC.
</p><p>The <a href="/wiki/Kingdom_of_Pontus" title="Kingdom of Pontus">Kingdom of Pontus</a> was a <a href="/wiki/Hellenistic_period" title="Hellenistic period">Hellenistic</a> kingdom, centered in the historical region of <a href="/wiki/Pontus_(region)" title="Pontus (region)">Pontus</a> and ruled by the <a href="/wiki/Mithridatic_dynasty" title="Mithridatic dynasty">Mithridatic dynasty</a> of <a href="/wiki/Persian_people" class="mw-redirect" title="Persian people">Persian</a> origin,<sup id="cite_ref-84" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-84">&#91;84&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-85" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-85">&#91;85&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-86" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-86">&#91;86&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-:0_87-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-:0-87">&#91;87&#93;</a></sup> which may have been directly related to <a href="/wiki/Darius_I" class="mw-redirect" title="Darius I">Darius the Great</a> and the <a href="/wiki/Achaemenid_dynasty" title="Achaemenid dynasty">Achaemenid dynasty</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-88" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-88">&#91;88&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-:0_87-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-:0-87">&#91;87&#93;</a></sup> The kingdom was proclaimed by <a href="/wiki/Mithridates_I_of_Pontus" title="Mithridates I of Pontus">Mithridates I</a> in 281 BC and lasted until its conquest by the Roman Republic in 63 BC. The Kingdom of Pontus reached its largest extent under <a href="/wiki/Mithridates_VI" class="mw-redirect" title="Mithridates VI">Mithridates VI</a> the Great, who conquered Colchis, Cappadocia, Bithynia, and the Greek colonies of the Tauric Chersonesos. After a long struggle with <a href="/wiki/Roman_Empire" title="Roman Empire">Rome</a> in the <a href="/wiki/Mithridatic_Wars" title="Mithridatic Wars">Mithridatic Wars</a>, Pontus was defeated.
</p><p>All <a href="/wiki/Ancient_regions_of_Anatolia" title="Ancient regions of Anatolia">ancient regions and territories</a> corresponding to modern Turkey eventually became part of the <a href="/wiki/Roman_Empire" title="Roman Empire">Roman Empire</a>, and many of them retained their historic <a href="/wiki/Ancient_regions_of_Anatolia#Classical_Age_regions_(circa_200_BC)" title="Ancient regions of Anatolia">names in classical antiquity</a> as <a href="/wiki/Roman_provinces" class="mw-redirect" title="Roman provinces">Roman provinces</a>.
</p>
<h3><span class="mw-headline" id="Early_Christian_and_Roman_period">Early Christian and Roman period</span></h3>
<link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1033289096"/><div role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">Further information: <a href="/wiki/Christianity_in_Turkey" title="Christianity in Turkey">Christianity in Turkey</a></div>
<link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1096954695/mw-parser-output/.tmulti"/><div class="thumb tmulti tright"><div class="thumbinner multiimageinner" style="width:256px;max-width:256px"><div class="trow"><div class="tsingle" style="width:254px;max-width:254px"><div class="thumbimage"><a href="/wiki/File:Justinian555AD.png" class="image"><img alt="" src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/9b/Justinian555AD.png/252px-Justinian555AD.png" decoding="async" width="252" height="137" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/9b/Justinian555AD.png/378px-Justinian555AD.png 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/9b/Justinian555AD.png/504px-Justinian555AD.png 2x" data-file-width="2111" data-file-height="1144" /></a></div><div class="thumbcaption">The <a href="/wiki/Byzantine_Empire" title="Byzantine Empire">Byzantine Empire</a> in 555 under <a href="/wiki/Justinian_the_Great" class="mw-redirect" title="Justinian the Great">Justinian the Great</a>, at its greatest extent since the fall of the Western Roman Empire.</div></div></div><div class="trow"><div class="tsingle" style="width:254px;max-width:254px"><div class="thumbimage"><a href="/wiki/File:Aya_Sophia_(7144824757).jpg" class="image"><img alt="" src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/0b/Aya_Sophia_%287144824757%29.jpg/252px-Aya_Sophia_%287144824757%29.jpg" decoding="async" width="252" height="126" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/0b/Aya_Sophia_%287144824757%29.jpg/378px-Aya_Sophia_%287144824757%29.jpg 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/0b/Aya_Sophia_%287144824757%29.jpg/504px-Aya_Sophia_%287144824757%29.jpg 2x" data-file-width="2449" data-file-height="1225" /></a></div><div class="thumbcaption">Originally a church, then a mosque, later a museum, and now a mosque again, the <a href="/wiki/Hagia_Sophia" title="Hagia Sophia">Hagia Sophia</a> in <a href="/wiki/Istanbul" title="Istanbul">Istanbul</a> was built by the <a href="/wiki/Byzantine_Empire" title="Byzantine Empire">Byzantine</a> emperor <a href="/wiki/Justinian_I" title="Justinian I">Justinian I</a> in 532–537.<sup id="cite_ref-89" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-89">&#91;89&#93;</a></sup></div></div></div></div></div>
<p>According to the <a href="/wiki/Acts_of_Apostles" class="mw-redirect" title="Acts of Apostles">Acts of Apostles</a>,<sup id="cite_ref-90" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-90">&#91;90&#93;</a></sup> <a href="/wiki/Antioch" title="Antioch">Antioch</a> (now <a href="/wiki/Antakya" title="Antakya">Antakya</a>), a city in southern Turkey, is where the followers of <a href="/wiki/Jesus" title="Jesus">Jesus</a> were <a href="/wiki/Early_Christianity" class="mw-redirect" title="Early Christianity">first called</a> "<a href="/wiki/Christians" title="Christians">Christians</a>". The city quickly became an important <a href="/wiki/Early_centers_of_Christianity" class="mw-redirect" title="Early centers of Christianity">center of Christianity</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-91" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-91">&#91;91&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-92" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-92">&#91;92&#93;</a></sup> <a href="/wiki/Paul_the_Apostle" title="Paul the Apostle">Apostle Paul</a> of <a href="/wiki/Tarsus,_Mersin" title="Tarsus, Mersin">Tarsus</a> traveled to <a href="/wiki/Ephesus" title="Ephesus">Ephesus</a> and stayed there for almost three years, probably working as a tentmaker.<sup id="cite_ref-93" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-93">&#91;93&#93;</a></sup> He is claimed to have performed numerous <a href="/wiki/Miracle" title="Miracle">miracles</a>, healing people and casting out demons, and he apparently organized missionary activity in other regions.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTECrossLivingstone2005St_Paul_94-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTECrossLivingstone2005St_Paul-94">&#91;94&#93;</a></sup> Paul left <a href="/wiki/Ephesus" title="Ephesus">Ephesus</a> after an attack from a local silversmith resulted in a pro-<a href="/wiki/Artemis" title="Artemis">Artemis</a> riot involving most of the city.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTECrossLivingstone2005St_Paul_94-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTECrossLivingstone2005St_Paul-94">&#91;94&#93;</a></sup> According to <a href="/wiki/John_the_Apostle#Extrabiblical_traditions" title="John the Apostle">extrabiblical traditions</a>, the <a href="/wiki/Assumption_of_Mary" title="Assumption of Mary">Assumption of Mary</a> took place in Ephesus, where <a href="/wiki/John_the_Apostle" title="John the Apostle">Apostle John</a> was also present. <a href="/wiki/Irenaeus" title="Irenaeus">Irenaeus</a> writes of "the church of Ephesus, founded by Paul, with John continuing with them until the times of <a href="/wiki/Trajan" title="Trajan">Trajan</a>."<sup id="cite_ref-95" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-95">&#91;95&#93;</a></sup> While in Ephesus, Apostle John wrote the <a href="/wiki/Johannine_epistles" title="Johannine epistles">three epistles</a> attributed to him. John was allegedly banished by the Roman authorities to the Greek island of <a href="/wiki/Patmos" title="Patmos">Patmos</a>, where, according to tradition, he wrote the <a href="/wiki/Book_of_Revelation" title="Book of Revelation">Book of Revelation</a>. The <a href="/wiki/Basilica_of_St._John" title="Basilica of St. John">Basilica of St. John</a> near Ephesus, built by <a href="/wiki/Justinian_I" title="Justinian I">Justinian the Great</a> in the 6th century, marks the <a href="/wiki/Basilica_of_St._John#St._John_in_Ephesus" title="Basilica of St. John">burial site of Apostle John</a>, while the nearby <a href="/wiki/House_of_the_Virgin_Mary" title="House of the Virgin Mary">House of the Virgin Mary</a> is accepted by the Catholic church as the place where <a href="/wiki/Mary,_mother_of_Jesus" title="Mary, mother of Jesus">Mary, mother of Jesus</a>, lived the final days of her life, before her <a href="/wiki/Assumption_of_Mary" title="Assumption of Mary">Assumption</a>. <a href="/wiki/Saint_Nicholas" title="Saint Nicholas">Saint Nicholas</a>, born in <a href="/wiki/Patara_(Lycia)" title="Patara (Lycia)">Patara</a>, lived in nearby <a href="/wiki/Myra" title="Myra">Myra</a> (modern <a href="/wiki/Demre" title="Demre">Demre</a>) in <a href="/wiki/Lycia" title="Lycia">Lycia</a>. 
</p><p>In the year 123, Emperor <a href="/wiki/Hadrian" title="Hadrian">Hadrian</a> traveled to <a href="/wiki/Anatolia" title="Anatolia">Anatolia</a>. Numerous monuments were erected for his arrival and he met his lover <a href="/wiki/Antinous" title="Antinous">Antinous</a> from <a href="/wiki/Bithynia" title="Bithynia">Bithynia</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-ahb_96-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-ahb-96">&#91;96&#93;</a></sup> <a href="/wiki/Hadrian" title="Hadrian">Hadrian</a> focused on the Greek revival and built several temples and improved the cities. <a href="/wiki/Cyzicus" title="Cyzicus">Cyzicus</a>, <a href="/wiki/Pergamon" title="Pergamon">Pergamon</a>, <a href="/wiki/Smyrna" title="Smyrna">Smyrna</a>, <a href="/wiki/Ephesus" title="Ephesus">Ephesus</a> and <a href="/wiki/Sardes" class="mw-redirect" title="Sardes">Sardes</a> were promoted as regional centres for the <a href="/wiki/Imperial_cult_(ancient_Rome)" class="mw-redirect" title="Imperial cult (ancient Rome)">Imperial cult</a> (<a href="/wiki/Neocorate" title="Neocorate"><i>neocoros</i></a>) during this period.<sup id="cite_ref-97" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-97">&#91;97&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<h3><span class="mw-headline" id="Byzantine_period">Byzantine period</span></h3>
<link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1033289096"/><div role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">Main article: <a href="/wiki/Byzantine_Anatolia" title="Byzantine Anatolia">Byzantine Anatolia</a></div>
<link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1033289096"/><div role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">Further information: <a href="/wiki/Byzantine_Empire" title="Byzantine Empire">Byzantine Empire</a></div>
<div class="thumb tleft"><div class="thumbinner" style="width:252px;"><a href="/wiki/File:Fethiye_Museum_9607.jpg" class="image"><img alt="" src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/88/Fethiye_Museum_9607.jpg/250px-Fethiye_Museum_9607.jpg" decoding="async" width="250" height="166" class="thumbimage" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/88/Fethiye_Museum_9607.jpg/375px-Fethiye_Museum_9607.jpg 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/88/Fethiye_Museum_9607.jpg/500px-Fethiye_Museum_9607.jpg 2x" data-file-width="1600" data-file-height="1065" /></a>  <div class="thumbcaption"><div class="magnify"><a href="/wiki/File:Fethiye_Museum_9607.jpg" class="internal" title="Enlarge"></a></div>Mosaic of <a href="/wiki/Jesus" title="Jesus">Jesus</a> at the <a href="/wiki/Pammakaristos_Church" title="Pammakaristos Church">Pammakaristos Church</a> in <a href="/wiki/Istanbul" title="Istanbul">Istanbul</a>. <a href="/wiki/Byzantine_mosaics" title="Byzantine mosaics">Byzantine mosaics</a> are the most celebrated form of <a href="/wiki/Byzantine_art" title="Byzantine art">Byzantine art</a>.</div></div></div>
<p>In 324 AD, <a href="/wiki/Constantine_I" class="mw-redirect" title="Constantine I">Constantine I</a> chose Byzantium to be the new capital of the Roman Empire, renaming it <a href="/wiki/New_Rome" title="New Rome">New Rome</a>. Under Constantine, Christianity did not become the exclusive religion of the state, but enjoyed imperial preference since <a href="/wiki/Constantine_the_Great_and_Christianity" title="Constantine the Great and Christianity">he supported it with generous privileges</a>. Following the death of <a href="/wiki/Theodosius_I" title="Theodosius I">Theodosius I</a> in 395 and the permanent division of the Roman Empire between his two sons, the city, which would popularly come to be known as <a href="/wiki/Constantinople" title="Constantinople">Constantinople</a>, became the capital of the <a href="/wiki/Eastern_Roman_Empire" class="mw-redirect" title="Eastern Roman Empire">Eastern Roman Empire</a>. This empire, which would later be branded by historians as the <a href="/wiki/Byzantine_Empire" title="Byzantine Empire">Byzantine Empire</a>, ruled most of the territory of present-day Turkey until the <a href="/wiki/Late_Middle_Ages" title="Late Middle Ages">Late Middle Ages</a>;<sup id="cite_ref-98" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-98">&#91;98&#93;</a></sup> although the eastern regions remained firmly in <a href="/wiki/Sasanian" class="mw-redirect" title="Sasanian">Sasanian</a> hands until the first half of the 7th century. The frequent <a href="/wiki/Byzantine-Sassanid_Wars" class="mw-redirect" title="Byzantine-Sassanid Wars">Byzantine-Sassanid Wars</a>, a continuation of the centuries-long <a href="/wiki/Roman-Persian_Wars" class="mw-redirect" title="Roman-Persian Wars">Roman-Persian Wars</a>, took place in various parts of present-day Turkey between the 4th and 7th centuries. Several <a href="/wiki/Ecumenical_councils" class="mw-redirect" title="Ecumenical councils">ecumenical councils</a> of the <a href="/wiki/Early_Church" class="mw-redirect" title="Early Church">early Church</a> were held in cities located in present-day Turkey, including the <a href="/wiki/First_Council_of_Nicaea" title="First Council of Nicaea">First Council of Nicaea</a> (<a href="/wiki/Iznik" class="mw-redirect" title="Iznik">Iznik</a>) in 325 (which resulted in the first uniform Christian <a href="/wiki/Doctrine" title="Doctrine">doctrine</a>, called the <a href="/wiki/Nicene_Creed" title="Nicene Creed">Nicene Creed</a>), the <a href="/wiki/First_Council_of_Constantinople" title="First Council of Constantinople">First Council of Constantinople</a> (Istanbul) in 381, the <a href="/wiki/Council_of_Ephesus" title="Council of Ephesus">Council of Ephesus</a> in 431, and the <a href="/wiki/Council_of_Chalcedon" title="Council of Chalcedon">Council of Chalcedon</a> (<a href="/wiki/Kad%C4%B1k%C3%B6y" title="Kadıköy">Kadıköy</a>) in 451.<sup id="cite_ref-99" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-99">&#91;99&#93;</a></sup> During most of its existence, the <a href="/wiki/Byzantine_Empire" title="Byzantine Empire">Byzantine Empire</a> was one of the most powerful economic, cultural, and military forces in Europe.<sup id="cite_ref-100" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-100">&#91;100&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<h3><span class="mw-headline" id="Seljuks_and_the_Ottoman_Empire">Seljuks and the Ottoman Empire</span></h3>
<link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1033289096"/><div role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">Further information: <a href="/wiki/Turkic_migration" title="Turkic migration">Turkic migration</a>, <a href="/wiki/Seljuk_Empire" title="Seljuk Empire">Seljuk Empire</a>, <a href="/wiki/Sultanate_of_Rum" title="Sultanate of Rum">Sultanate of Rum</a>, and <a href="/wiki/Ottoman_Empire" title="Ottoman Empire">Ottoman Empire</a></div>
<div class="thumb tright"><div class="thumbinner" style="width:252px;"><a href="/wiki/File:Seljuk_Empire_locator_map.svg" class="image"><img alt="" src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/c3/Seljuk_Empire_locator_map.svg/250px-Seljuk_Empire_locator_map.svg.png" decoding="async" width="250" height="153" class="thumbimage" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/c3/Seljuk_Empire_locator_map.svg/375px-Seljuk_Empire_locator_map.svg.png 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/c3/Seljuk_Empire_locator_map.svg/500px-Seljuk_Empire_locator_map.svg.png 2x" data-file-width="800" data-file-height="488" /></a>  <div class="thumbcaption"><div class="magnify"><a href="/wiki/File:Seljuk_Empire_locator_map.svg" class="internal" title="Enlarge"></a></div>The <a href="/wiki/Great_Seljuk_Empire" class="mw-redirect" title="Great Seljuk Empire">Great Seljuk Empire</a> in 1092, upon the death of <a href="/wiki/Malik_Shah_I" class="mw-redirect" title="Malik Shah I">Malik Shah I</a><sup id="cite_ref-101" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-101">&#91;101&#93;</a></sup></div></div></div>
<p>The <a href="/wiki/Seljuq_dynasty" class="mw-redirect" title="Seljuq dynasty">House of Seljuk</a> originated from the <i><a href="/wiki/K%C4%B1n%C4%B1k_(tribe)" class="mw-redirect" title="Kınık (tribe)">Kınık</a></i> branch of the <a href="/wiki/Oghuz_Turks" title="Oghuz Turks">Oghuz Turks</a> who resided on the periphery of the <a href="/wiki/Muslim_history#Abbasids_-_&quot;Islamic_Golden_Age&quot;" class="mw-redirect" title="Muslim history">Muslim world</a>, in the <a href="/wiki/Oghuz_Yabgu_State" title="Oghuz Yabgu State">Yabgu Khaganate</a> of the Oğuz confederacy, to the north of the <a href="/wiki/Caspian_Sea" title="Caspian Sea">Caspian</a> and <a href="/wiki/Aral_Sea" title="Aral Sea">Aral Seas</a>, in the 9th century.<sup id="cite_ref-102" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-102">&#91;102&#93;</a></sup> In the 10th century, the Seljuks started migrating from their ancestral homeland into <a href="/wiki/Persia" class="mw-redirect" title="Persia">Persia</a>, which became the administrative core of the <a href="/wiki/Seljuk_Empire" title="Seljuk Empire">Great Seljuk Empire</a>, after its foundation by <a href="/wiki/Tughril" title="Tughril">Tughril</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-peter.mackenzie.org_103-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-peter.mackenzie.org-103">&#91;103&#93;</a></sup>
In the latter half of the 11th century, the Seljuk Turks began penetrating into <a href="/wiki/Medieval_Armenia" title="Medieval Armenia">medieval Armenia</a> and the eastern regions of Anatolia. In 1071, the Seljuks defeated the Byzantines at the <a href="/wiki/Battle_of_Manzikert" title="Battle of Manzikert">Battle of Manzikert</a>, starting the <a href="/wiki/Turkification" title="Turkification">Turkification</a> process in the area; the Turkish language and <a href="/wiki/Islam" title="Islam">Islam</a> were introduced to Anatolia, gradually spreading throughout the region. The slow transition from a predominantly <a href="/wiki/Christians" title="Christians">Christian</a> and <a href="/wiki/Greek_language" title="Greek language">Greek</a>-speaking Anatolia to a predominantly <a href="/wiki/Muslim" class="mw-redirect" title="Muslim">Muslim</a> and Turkish-speaking one was underway. 
</p><p>The <a href="/wiki/Mevlevi_Order" title="Mevlevi Order">Mevlevi Order</a> of <a href="/wiki/Dervishes" class="mw-redirect" title="Dervishes">dervishes</a>, which was established in <a href="/wiki/Konya" title="Konya">Konya</a> during the 13th century by <a href="/wiki/Sufi" class="mw-redirect" title="Sufi">Sufi</a> poet <a href="/wiki/Rumi" title="Rumi">Mevlânâ Rûmî</a>, played a significant role in the <a href="/wiki/Islamization" title="Islamization">Islamization</a> of the diverse people of Anatolia who had previously been <a href="/wiki/Hellenized" class="mw-redirect" title="Hellenized">Hellenized</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-104" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-104">&#91;104&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-105" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-105">&#91;105&#93;</a></sup> Thus, alongside the Turkification of the territory, the <a href="/wiki/Persianate_society" title="Persianate society">culturally Persianized</a> Seljuks set the basis for a <a href="/wiki/Turko-Persian_tradition" class="mw-redirect" title="Turko-Persian tradition">Turko-Persian principal culture</a> in Anatolia,<sup id="cite_ref-106" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-106">&#91;106&#93;</a></sup> which their eventual successors, <a href="/wiki/Culture_of_the_Ottoman_Empire" title="Culture of the Ottoman Empire">the Ottomans</a>, would take over.<sup id="cite_ref-107" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-107">&#91;107&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-108" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-108">&#91;108&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1096954695/mw-parser-output/.tmulti"/><div class="thumb tmulti tright"><div class="thumbinner multiimageinner" style="width:342px;max-width:342px"><div class="trow"><div class="tsingle" style="width:106px;max-width:106px"><div class="thumbimage"><a href="/wiki/File:Ince_Minareli_Medrese_02.jpg" class="image"><img alt="" src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/27/Ince_Minareli_Medrese_02.jpg/104px-Ince_Minareli_Medrese_02.jpg" decoding="async" width="104" height="142" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/27/Ince_Minareli_Medrese_02.jpg/156px-Ince_Minareli_Medrese_02.jpg 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/27/Ince_Minareli_Medrese_02.jpg/208px-Ince_Minareli_Medrese_02.jpg 2x" data-file-width="2524" data-file-height="3437" /></a></div></div><div class="tsingle" style="width:122px;max-width:122px"><div class="thumbimage"><a href="/wiki/File:%C3%87ifte_Minareli_Medrese_(Erzurum)_Entrance_8685_(cropped).jpg" class="image"><img alt="" src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/98/%C3%87ifte_Minareli_Medrese_%28Erzurum%29_Entrance_8685_%28cropped%29.jpg/120px-%C3%87ifte_Minareli_Medrese_%28Erzurum%29_Entrance_8685_%28cropped%29.jpg" decoding="async" width="120" height="141" 2x" data-file-width="2832" data-file-height="3326" /></a></div></div><div class="tsingle" style="width:108px;max-width:108px"><div class="thumbimage"><a href="/wiki/File:Divrigi_Hospital_portal_DSCF3199.jpg" class="image"><img alt="" src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/4e/Divrigi_Hospital_portal_DSCF3199.jpg/106px-Divrigi_Hospital_portal_DSCF3199.jpg" decoding="async" width="106" height="141"
